system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Positive almost-sure termination
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The distinction between almost-sure termination (termination probability 1) and positive almost-sure termination (finite expected runtime), with the random-walk and geometric-loop examples, the implication from finite expected runtime to almost-sure termination and its failure in reverse, the non-compositionality of the property, and its arithmetical-hierarchy hardness as reported in the book. Excludes the martingale and ert proof techniques themselves.

ATOMS:
- CS-PL-C02-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A closed term $M$ of the probabilistic $\lambda$-calculus is positively almost surely terminating if and only if its expected reduction length (the average number of reduction steps) satisfies $\mathrm{ExLen}(M) < +\infty$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0151-s16] As a consequence, the average number of reduction steps ExLen(M) for M is defined as follows:
    [CS-PL-p0151-s19] We say that M is positively almost surely terminating if ExLen(M) < +∞.
- CS-PL-C02-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: For a closed term $M$, where $T$ is the random variable counting the number of steps $M$ requires to be reduced to a value, the expected reduction length is defined as $\mathrm{ExLen}(M) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\Pr(T>m) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(1-\sum_{n=0}^{m}\|\langle M\rangle_n\|\right)$, where $\sum_{n=0}^{m}\|\langle M\rangle_n\|$ is the probability that $M$ reduces to a value in at most $m$ reduction steps.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0151-s12] As already mentioned in Section 4.2, a convenient way to define it is as
    [CS-PL-p0151-s13] where T is the random variable counting the number of steps M requires to be reduced to a value.
- CS-PL-C02-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A term $M$ is almost surely terminating if $\|\langle M\rangle\| = 1$, that is, if its probability of convergence is 1.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0151-s01] that M is almost surely terminating if ∥⟨M⟩∥= 1, namely if its probability of convergence is 1.
- CS-PL-C02-S1-04 | S1
  ATOM: A probabilistic program is almost-surely terminating when all of its infinite runs have probability zero, equivalently when its probability of termination is one.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0207-s17] A more sensible notion of termination might thus require that all infinite runs of a program have probability zero.
    [CS-PL-p0207-s18] Conversely: The probability of termination is one.
    [CS-PL-p0207-s19] This is referred to as almost-sure termination (Hart et al., 1983).
- CS-PL-C02-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: The decision problem of whether a probabilistic program terminates in finite expected time (on all inputs) is $\Pi^0_3$-complete in the arithmetical hierarchy, and is thus strictly harder than the universal halting problem for ordinary programs.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0208-s10] From a complexity-theoretic view, it is noteworthy that the decision problem “does a program terminate in finite expected time (on all inputs)?” is Π0 3complete in the arithmetical hierarchy, and thus strictly harder than the universal halting problem for ordinary programs (Kaminski and Katoen, 2015; Kaminski et al., 2018a).
- CS-PL-C02-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: For probabilistic programs, having a finite expected runtime (positive almost-sure termination) implies almost-sure termination.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0208-s08] In fact, having a finite expected runtime implies almost-sure termination (Olmedo et al., 2016, Theorem 5.3).
- CS-PL-C02-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Every positively almost-surely terminating term is almost-surely terminating, because finiteness of the expected reduction length requires $\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{m}\|\langle M\rangle_n\| = 1$, which can hold only if $\|\langle M\rangle\| = 1$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0151-s21] Lemma 4.24. Every positively almost-surely terminating term is almost-surely terminating.
    [CS-PL-p0152-s01] Proof A necessary condition for ExLen(M) to be finite is that
    [CS-PL-p0152-s02] which can hold only if ∥⟨M⟩∥= 1, namely only if M is almost surely terminating. □
- CS-PL-C02-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Positive almost-sure termination is not closed under sequential composition: there are two probabilistic programs $c_1$ and $c_2$, each positively almost-surely terminating, whose sequential composition $c_1; c_2$ has infinite expected runtime even though it almost-surely terminates, whereas termination of ordinary programs is closed under sequential composition.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0208-s14] This is not true for probabilistic programs when considering positive almost-sure termination.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s16] Both programs terminate positive almost-surely: As the loop in C1 terminates on average in two iterations, it has a finite expected runtime.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s17] Furthermore, program c2 performs at most ⌈x⌉iterations for any initial value of x, i.e. its expected runtime is finite, too.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s18] However, the composed program c1; c2 has an infinite expected runtime – even though it almost-surely terminates.
- CS-PL-C02-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Almost-sure termination does not imply positive almost-sure termination: the one-dimensional random-walk program that starts at position 10 and in each step moves one step left or right at random until reaching position 0 reaches position 0 with probability one, yet requires infinitely many steps on average, so its expected runtime is infinite.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0208-s01] which models a one-dimensional random walk of a particle: Starting from position 10, in each step the particle moves randomly one step to the left or one step to the right, until reaching position 0.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s02] The particle reaches position 0 with probability one.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s03] The program crw thus terminates almost-surely.
    [CS-PL-p0208-s04] However, doing so requires infinitely many steps on average (cf. Ibe, 2013, Chapter 3.7.3).
    [CS-PL-p0208-s05] The expected runtime of crw is thus infinite.
- CS-PL-C02-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: A probabilistic program can have a finite expected runtime even though it admits arbitrarily long runs and even a non-terminating run: the program that flips a fair coin repeatedly until the first heads has a geometrically distributed runtime, and it terminates after two loop iterations on average, although the all-tails run is non-terminating (with probability zero).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0207-s09] They may admit arbitrarily long and even infinite runs while still having a finite expected runtime.
    [CS-PL-p0207-s11] keeps flipping a fair coin until observing the first heads (represented by 0).
    [CS-PL-p0207-s12] It admits arbitrarily long runs, since – for every natural number n – the probability of not seeing a heads in the first n trials is non-zero.
    [CS-PL-p0207-s13] It even admits a non-terminating run, namely the one in which the outcome of all coin flips is tails.
    [CS-PL-p0207-s14] The runtime of program cgeo, however, is geometrically distributed and therefore its expected runtime is finite, even constant: On average, it terminates after two loop iterations.
